newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht hit by dollar, devaluation fear.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht hit by dollar, devaluation fear.

text.p: * Thai baht under pressure again as dollar renews rally against majors. Fears of devaluation following erroneous wire service report also trigger baht sales.
* Malaysian ringgit shrugs off dollar strength in face of continued ringgit/Singapore dollar buying and reports of comment by Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister.
* Singapore dollar edges towards 1.42 level as ringgit/Sing cross breaches 0.5700 on continued buying across-the-board.
* Indonesian rupiah firms as players sell spot dollars to capture weekend premiums by covering back on Thursday.

The Thai baht remained prey to the current climate of bearish sentiment on Wednesday, as offshore players continued to unload the currency despite the previous day's announcement of spending cuts by the government.
The dollar's renewed rally against the major currencies also sparked a baht sell-off by offshore speculators, taking the Thai unit to a low of 26.01 to the dollar in early trade.
The baht was quoted at 25.990-25.995 at 0445 GMT against 25.925/25.935 late on Tuesday.
The Bank of Thailand (BOT) set the mid-rate at 25.96 to the dollar, the lowest level since May 4, 1990 when it was at 26.00 per dollar.

"Offshore players took the opportunity of dollar's rise abroad to sell off the baht again this morning. They may want to test the central bank's ability to defend the currency," said a dealer at a foreign bank in Bangkok.

Singapore dealers said the baht's fall was partly triggered by an erroneous wire service report quoting the Thai Commerce Minister telling a Thai newspaper a baht devaluation was possible within the next six months.
The news wire then corrected the report, attributing the statement to a recent research paper by Goldman Sachs, rather than the Commerce Minister.

"When the news came out, people panicked a bit and pushed the spot to 26.01," said a U.S. bank dealer, adding that the baht was not likely to fall below 26.02 on Wednesday unless there was fresh news to rock the market.
He said the baht's sudden recovery to 26.00 after falling below that level suggested possible BOT intervention, but added that he had not seen any signs of the central bank.
Market talk of BOT intervention late on Tuesday afternoon significantly helped strengthen the baht against the dollar, dealers said.
The heavy buying of the dollar tightened liquidity in the banking system in early trade on Wednesday causing the overnight interbank rate to rise to 13.00-14.00 percent.

"The strong buying of the dollar squeezed the money supply again. Most local banks were reluctant to lend funds and maintained their money to speculate in the foreign exchange market," said a money market dealer at a foreign bank in Bangkok.

Dealers said Thai asset markets had found little solace in the government's announcement on Tuesday that it would make 99 billion baht worth of spending cuts in fiscal 1996/97 to help narrow the current account deficit.
Kate O'Donoghue, economist at Sassoon Securities in Hong Kong told Reuters Financial Television, the nature of the cuts would determine how investors reacted to them.

"If they cut it by cutting back on military expenditure, that will be very positive. However, if it's just cosmetic changes...or if they cut back investment on essential infrastructure, that's not quite so positive," she said.

In Malaysia, the ringgit shrugged off the dollar's strength as a ringgit/Singapore dollar buying spree set in motion on Tuesday gathered steam, propelling the cross rate through the 0.5700 level, not seen since July 1996.
Dealers said comments by Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim that Malaysia was not worried by the rising ringgit were also keeping the local unit steady.

"The economy is strong and the ringgit seems to be strengthening against the U.S. dollar. I don't think it is an issue that should be highlighted or be overly concerned about," the daily New Straits Times quoted him as saying.
"The ringgit is not reacting to the strong dollar because of Anwar's comments," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.
He said the ringgit would remain rangebound because of the strength of the U.S. dollar against other major currencies.
The ringgit resumed its climb against the dollar this week after a fortnight-long correction phase, mainly due to buying against the low-yielding Singapore dollar.
Further south, the Singapore dollar bowed to its neighbour's strength, edging towards a one-year low of S$1.4200 against the U.S. dollar.
But dealers said commercial U.S. dollar selling interest around the S$1.4190 level was slowing the Singapore dollar's decline.
"For the moment, we don't see (the U.S. dollar) going above 1.42 but when London comes in, it'll be a different market altogether," said a local bank dealer.
Dealers said the U.S. dollar would be picked up on any dips to S$1.4150 and below by players who had missed the currency's run-up on Tuesday.
The Indonesian rupiah firmed in slow trade with many players still away after a two-day holiday to celebrate the Chinese and Moslem new years.
A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said Hong Kong and local operators were seen unloading spot dollars in the morning to capture weekend premiums when they cover back on Thursday.
Spot value on Thursday will have a longer maturity due to a public holiday in the United States next Monday.
But he added that sustained uncertainty over the Thai baht seemed to cause some covering in dollars by offshore players.
Spot rupiah was quoted at 2,376.7/77.2 at 0445 GMT, compared with an opening of 2,376.75/77.50.
Dealers said short-term swaps edged up on buying from Hong Kong players, enabling local operators to arbitrage with the cheaper money market rates. Longer-term swaps were stable.
-- Madhav Reddy in KL (603-230 8911), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
